docs.title: About Me
docs.text:
My name is Efe. I am a student interested in mechanical engineering, vehicle systems, materials, and understanding how technical designs become physical objects.

I want to use digital fabrication to improve my ability to design, manufacture, test, and refine prototypes. This website records the methods and reasoning behind my work.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
• Produce reproducible technical documentation.
  • Connect digital design with manufacturing.
  • Evaluate prototypes using measurements and observations.
  • Use version control to preserve project history.

docs.title: Assignment 2 — Modular 3D Rocket
docs.text:
Project: Design and manufacture a detachable 3D-printed rocket kit CAD software: Onshape Current progress: CAD design and STL exports completed; physical printing and photographic evidence pending.

Project status

I have completed the rocket model in Onshape and exported the individual Part Studio and assembled Assembly STL files. The physical 3D print has not yet been completed or documented. Print settings, photographs, and fit-test results will be added after manufacturing.

docs.title: 1. What was the goal?
docs.text:
The goal was to create a modular rocket as a three-dimensional CAD model and manufacture it using a 3D printer. The rocket needs to function as a detachable kit whose components can be assembled and removed. The teacher clarified that pins are not mandatory, provided the design remains detachable.

Another objective was to make the work reproducible by publishing the 3D source exports as a downloadable ZIP, together with a description of the design, manufacturing process, observations, and photographs of the printed result.

docs.title: 2. What did I do?
docs.text:
I designed the rocket in Onshape, separating the design into components rather than treating the entire object as a permanently fused part. I developed the rocket's main body geometry and connection features, and created assembled views to examine how the pieces fit together.

I exported nine Part Studio STL files and two Assembly STL files. These exports are included in the project's downloadable-file package, which will be published in the assets folder.

The STL files contain triangle meshes suitable for importing into slicer software. The assembly exports are useful for visualizing the assembled design; the individual part exports are more appropriate for planning detachable printing.

docs.title: Recorded STL exports
docs.text:
File Approximate bounding-box dimensions* Purpose Part Studio 1.stl 3.4 × 3.4 × 9.0 mm Individual component Part Studio 2.stl 15.2 × 7.5 × 35.1 mm Individual component Part Studio 3.stl 28.8 × 28.8 × 59.9 mm Individual component Part Studio 4.stl 8.4 × 8.4 × 15.2 mm Individual component Part Studio 5.stl 28.8 × 28.8 × 36.0 mm Individual component Part Studio 6.stl 14.3 × 14.3 × 37.6 mm Individual component Part Studio 7.stl 28.8 × 28.8 × 18.0 mm Individual component Part Studio 8.stl 8.4 × 8.4 × 33.0 mm Individual component Part Studio 9.stl 14.3 × 14.3 × 55.0 mm Individual export requiring mesh review Assembly 1.stl 59.2 × 59.2 × 205.7 mm Assembled export Assembly 2.stl 105.5 × 60.5 × 59.9 mm Additional assembly export

Dimensions are measured from the STL mesh bounds, rounded to 0.1 mm. They describe each file's full extents, not necessarily the nominal CAD dimensions. They assume the exported coordinates are in millimeters.

Mesh validation before printing

A preliminary mesh inspection found that Part Studio 9.stl is not watertight, and both assembled exports contain multiple shells or mesh irregularities. This alone does not prove the design is unprintable, but the affected models should be examined in slicer preview and repaired or re-exported if required. No successful test print has yet been confirmed.

docs.title: 3. What tools and materials did I use?
docs.text: Tool / material Use Onshape CAD modeling and assembly construction STL Exporting geometric meshes for slicing and sharing GitHub Storing documentation and published project files MkDocs + Material Generating the documentation website GitHub Pages Making the project documentation publicly accessible 3D printer and slicer To be identified and documented after printing Filament or resin To be recorded once the actual printer and material are known

docs.title: 4. How does the detachable design work?
docs.text:
The rocket was designed as a multi-part kit. The geometry includes cylindrical connector features and separate structural sections. The intent is to allow the components to be fitted together and taken apart rather than printing the entire assembly as a single inseparable object.

The actual fit, clearance, and ease of disassembly must be tested on the physical print. A nominal match between a peg and a hole in CAD does not guarantee a functional fit after manufacturing: machine calibration, print orientation, and material behavior all affect the outcome.

docs.title: 5. What went wrong? What did I change?
docs.text:
During CAD: The design was divided into multiple models and assemblies so that connections and relative placement could be considered separately. Specific modeling failures or redesigns should be added here only if verified from the design history.

During export review: A preliminary mesh check highlighted an open or multi-shell export in Part Studio 9.stl. I will examine that file in the slicer or re-export it from Onshape if it causes a slicing error.

During printing: Not attempted or documented yet. I will record failed prints, dimensional mismatches, support issues, and any design revisions after testing.

docs.title: 6. Preparing the 3D print
docs.text:
Once the printer model is known, I will:

  1. Select the exact printer and material profile in its slicer.
  2. Import the individual components instead of attempting to print an already assembled model as one object.
  3. Orient the parts for stability and manageable support removal.
  4. Check scale, toolpaths, and small connection features in slicer preview.
  5. Test a representative connection before printing the entire kit, if practical.
  6. Print the components, remove supports, and test the assembly.

These are planned actions, not completed manufacturing results.

docs.title: 7. Open-source design files
docs.text:
I have exported the model as 11 STL files: nine Part Studio exports and two Assembly exports. They have been collected into the ZIP archive Efe_Modular_Rocket_STL_Files.zip.

File publication: The ZIP has been prepared but still needs to be uploaded to this GitHub repository. After upload, this section will contain the direct download link. The STL files are mesh exports; an editable Onshape project link or STEP exports could also be added later for easier modification.

docs.title: 9. What was the result?
docs.text:
Current result: A completed digital rocket model in Onshape, with individual and assembled STL exports prepared for manufacturing and open-source sharing.

Remaining result to document: A successfully printed, detachable rocket and photographs demonstrating that its components can be assembled and removed.

The final manufacturing result, printer settings, and any fit adjustments will be recorded here after the physical print is complete.

docs.title: Week 1 — Website Development
docs.text:
Goal: Create a documentation website using GitHub Pages, Markdown, and MkDocs.

Website published and documented

The GitHub repository, successful deployment, Obsidian setup, and published website are documented with screenshots below. Local Markdown editing and synchronization through Git remain optional next steps to practise.

docs.title: 1. Understanding the tools
docs.text: Tool Function Git Records file changes and versions GitHub Hosts the project repository GitHub Pages Serves a public website Obsidian Edits Markdown documentation MkDocs Converts Markdown into static HTML Material for MkDocs Provides navigation, search and styling

docs.title: 2. Choosing MkDocs
docs.text: MkDocs suits documentation websites because it uses readable Markdown files. The Material theme supplies responsive navigation, search, and light/dark modes. The source is separate from the published HTML, which is generated automatically.

docs.title: 3. Repository structure
docs.text:
digital-fabrication/
├── .github/workflows/deploy.yml
├── docs/
│   ├── index.md
│   ├── about.md
│   ├── week-1.md
│   ├── projects.md
│   └── resources.md
├── mkdocs.yml
└── requirements.txt

The docs folder contains Markdown documents. mkdocs.yml defines the website theme and navigation. The GitHub Actions workflow builds the site.

docs.title: 4. Publication procedure
docs.text:
1. Create a public GitHub repository named digital-fabrication.
  2. Add the MkDocs configuration, Markdown pages, and GitHub Actions workflow.
  3. Open Actions and check whether Deploy MkDocs to GitHub Pages completes successfully.
  4. In Settings → Pages, select Deploy from a branch, gh-pages, and / (root).
  5. Visit the final website.
Markdown → GitHub commit → GitHub Actions → MkDocs build
→ gh-pages branch → published website

docs.title: 5. Using Obsidian
docs.text:
I installed Obsidian to work with Markdown documentation files. After downloading my GitHub repository as a ZIP file and extracting it, I opened the project folder as a vault in Obsidian.

I was then able to access and view the Markdown files, including week-1.md, which contains the documentation for this assignment.

Although Obsidian allows me to edit these files locally, changes are not automatically synchronized with GitHub because I downloaded the repository as a ZIP file rather than cloning it using Git. To update the published website, I need to upload the modified files to GitHub, where GitHub Actions automatically rebuilds and deploys the website.

docs.title: 6. Optional local preview
docs.text:
With Python installed, run from the repository directory:

python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python -m mkdocs serve

Open http://127.0.0.1:8000/.

Other useful Git commands:

git status
git add .
git commit -m "Update documentation"
git push

docs.title: 7. Evidence from the website setup
docs.text: The screenshots below show the repository, successful publishing workflow, Obsidian editor, and completed website. All four images are stored in this repository.

docs.title: GitHub repository
docs.text: The repository named gaminghub492/digital-fabrication contains the Markdown documentation in docs/, a mkdocs.yml configuration file, the package requirements, and the automated workflow under .github/workflows/. This separation keeps editable source files distinct from the generated website.

docs.title: GitHub Actions and deployment
docs.text: The Actions page shows the Prevent concurrent MkDocs Pages deployments workflow completing successfully, alongside the GitHub Pages publishing workflow. Each update to the main branch can trigger a rebuild, so changes to the documentation can appear on the public website without manually uploading generated HTML.

docs.title: Editing documentation using Obsidian
docs.text: I installed Obsidian, downloaded and extracted the documentation project, and opened it as a vault. The editor displays week-1.md alongside the other Markdown pages. Markdown headings, tables, and text can be edited directly. Because this is an extracted ZIP rather than a Git clone, changes saved locally do not automatically update GitHub.

docs.title: Published MkDocs website
docs.text: The public site at Efe | Digital Fabrication displays the Material for MkDocs theme and navigation for Home, About, Week 1, Future Projects, and Resources. This confirms the generated website is publicly viewable.

docs.title: Problem encountered and solution
docs.text:
During initial setup, the website source files were committed separately in quick succession. This triggered overlapping GitHub Actions runs, several of which attempted to publish to the gh-pages branch at nearly the same time. The error log showed a rejected push to gh-pages, because its branch reference had changed since a deployment started. In other words, the website build itself succeeded, but competing deployments interfered with publishing.

The workflow was updated to use a concurrency group that prevents simultaneous publishing jobs, and to retrieve full Git history. A subsequent run completed successfully, and the MkDocs website became accessible.

What I learned: Git tracks versions of source files; GitHub stores those files online; Obsidian edits Markdown; MkDocs generates a website from Markdown; and GitHub Actions with GitHub Pages publishes the resulting site. The deployment problem demonstrated why automated publishing jobs should not overwrite the same branch concurrently.

docs.title: 8. Completion checklist and reflection
docs.text:
• [x] Created the public GitHub repository.
  • [x] Uploaded the website source and documented its structure.
  • [x] Confirmed successful deployment and recorded a screenshot.
  • [x] Opened and photographed the published website.
  • [x] Installed Obsidian and opened the downloaded Markdown documentation.
  • [x] Documented the deployment error and its solution.
  • [x] Added the four evidence screenshots to the Week 1 documentation.
  • [ ] Practise making and saving a new change in Obsidian, then upload that change to GitHub. This is a future practice step, not a claim of completed work.

docs.title: Reflection
docs.text:
What worked? The source files were organized in GitHub, MkDocs generated the documentation website, and GitHub Pages made it available publicly. A successful deployment and screenshots of the finished site confirmed the outcome.

What problems occurred? Several overlapping GitHub Actions runs attempted to update the same gh-pages branch, leading to rejected pushes. Setting a concurrency group for publishing resolved the conflict.

What did I learn? Markdown provides a simple format for recording technical work, while MkDocs transforms it into a navigable website. GitHub stores the source and its revision history, and GitHub Actions automates publication. Obsidian can be used to edit the local Markdown files, but a downloaded ZIP does not automatically synchronize changes to GitHub.

See Resources for the course materials.
